title: Quirks of the Mind · Episode 1
chapters: The invisible gorilla: why we miss what's in front of us

units.t: Quirks of the Mind. Episode one.
In this episode: False memories, Why optical illusions fool you and The invisible gorilla: why we miss what's in front of us.
Part one. False memories.
Your memory isn't a recording.
It's a reconstruction, and it can be changed, or even invented, without you noticing.
Memory rebuilds, not replays.
We imagine memory as a video we replay.
In reality the brain stores fragments, such as a sight, a feeling or the gist of what was said.
It rebuilds the memory each time we recall it, filling gaps with expectations, later information and imagination.
Every recall is a chance for the memory to shift.
In the 1930s, British psychologist Frederic Bartlett showed people retelling an unfamiliar folk tale gradually reshaped it to fit their own culture's expectations.
That's why two people at the same event remember it differently, and why vivid, confident memories can still be wrong.
Words that never were.
You can test this in a minute.
In a method developed by James Deese and later Henry Roediger and Kathleen McDermott in 1995, people hear a list such as bed, rest, awake, tired, dream, snooze, blanket and nap.
Later, many confidently remember hearing 'sleep', which was never on the list.
Some even say they can picture it being read out.
The brain stores the theme and fills in what 'should' be there.
This harmless lab trick shows the process behind more serious false memories: plausible details slot in smoothly and feel just as real as genuine ones.
Suggestion rewrites memory.
In a 1978 study, Elizabeth Loftus and colleagues showed slides of a car stopped at a stop sign before hitting a pedestrian.
Some people were later asked a question that casually mentioned a 'yield', give way, sign.
They were far more likely to pick the wrong sign, often confidently.
This misinformation effect has been reproduced many times.
In the 1990s, Loftus and Jacqueline Pickrell invented a childhood event, being lost in a shopping mall, and presented it among real ones.
After repeated interviews, about a quarter of participants came to remember it, at least partly.
Researchers debate how many were full memories rather than vague beliefs, but memory can be fabricated, not just distorted.
Confidence is not accuracy.
Many people feel they remember exactly where they were when they heard shocking news, like the September 11 attacks.
These flashbulb memories change too.
After the 1986 Challenger disaster, Ulric Neisser asked students how they'd heard, then asked again about two and a half years later, and many accounts had changed dramatically.
A study of 9/11 recollections found the same: stories shifted, but confidence stayed high.
The US Innocence Project found that mistaken eyewitness identification played a role in around 70 per cent of convictions later overturned by DNA evidence.
Stress, leading questions and long delays reduce accuracy, and confidence grows if police confirm a pick.
Line-up procedures have since been reformed.
Holding memory lightly.
In the 1980s and 1990s, some therapists used hypnosis and guided imagery to help clients 'recover' memories of childhood abuse.
Some led to accusations and were later retracted.
Loftus argued such techniques could create false memories; others stressed that real abuse is common and often undisclosed for years.
This 'memory wars' debate led professional bodies to caution against suggestive techniques, while affirming that survivors deserve to be taken seriously.
Reconstruction is a design, not a flaw: it lets us learn and imagine the future.
But hold memories lightly.
Write down what a doctor, landlord or employer tells you.
In a disagreement, both people may be partly wrong without lying.
When asking others, especially children, use open questions like 'What happened next?'
, not leading ones.
The key idea: Each time you remember something, your brain reconstructs it from fragments and can change it.
Part two. Why optical illusions fool you.
Illusions aren't failures of your eyes.
They're your brain's clever shortcuts, caught in the act.
You see with your brain.
Your eyes send the brain a flat, patchy, constantly shifting image.
Only a small central area of each retina sees fine detail, and your eyes dart around several times a second.
The brain builds a stable 3D world by making assumptions: light comes from above, objects keep their size, nearby edges belong together.
These shortcuts work so well that we never notice them.
Optical illusions are situations where the assumptions give the wrong answer.
They're valuable to scientists because they reveal how much of seeing is interpretation rather than simple recording.
Size and shade tricks.
In the Müller-Lyer illusion, 1889, a line with outward fins looks longer than an identical line capped with arrowheads.
One theory is that the brain reads the shapes as corners near or far, and adjusts perceived size for distance.
In Edward Adelson's 1995 checker-shadow illusion, a square in shadow looks much lighter than a square in light, though they're exactly the same shade.
The brain corrects for shadows so objects keep a consistent colour: a white shirt still looks white under a tree.
This colour constancy also explains 'the dress' of 2015, which some saw as blue and black and others as white and gold.
It was actually blue and black; viewers differed in the lighting their brain assumed.
The moon illusion.
A rising full moon can look enormous, yet high in the sky it seems small.
Photographs show its image is essentially the same size in both positions.
If anything it is very slightly smaller at the horizon, because it's a little further from you.
The illusion has been discussed since ancient times, and there's still no single agreed explanation.
Leading ideas involve the brain treating the horizon as further away than the sky overhead, so it scales the moon up, and comparisons with trees and buildings nearby.
Try viewing a horizon moon through a rolled-up tube: it often shrinks.
Motion and flipping images.
In Akiyoshi Kitaoka's 'rotating snakes', a still image appears to swirl.
Researchers think tiny eye movements and the different speeds at which brain cells respond to light and dark produce a false motion signal.
Cinema uses a related trick: still frames shown in quick succession, usually 24 per second, are seen as smooth movement.
The Rubin vase, described around 1915, shows either a vase or two faces in profile, but hardly both at once.
The duck-rabbit and the Necker cube work the same way.
The image on your retina never changes; only your interpretation does.
The brain picks one reading and commits, then switches, and knowing the trick doesn't stop it.
Blind spots and other senses.
Where the optic nerve leaves each eye, there are no light-sensitive cells.
This blind spot is roughly ten times wider than the full moon appears.
You never notice it, partly because each eye covers the other's gap, and partly because the brain fills the hole with the surrounding colour or pattern.
Close one eye and move a small dot across a page until it vanishes.
Other senses are fooled too.
In the McGurk effect, 1976, lips saying 'ga' with audio of 'ba' often sound like 'da'.
In the size-weight illusion, a small object feels heavier than a large one of equal weight.
The lesson: feeling certain of what you perceive doesn't make it accurate.
The key idea: Vision is the brain's best guess about the world, built from limited information, and illusions expose its shortcuts.
Part three. The invisible gorilla: why we miss what's in front of us.
Half the people in a famous experiment failed to notice a gorilla walking through a basketball game.
They weren't careless.
They were human, and so are you.
The gorilla nobody saw.
In 1999, psychologists Daniel Simons and Christopher Chabris made a short video of students passing basketballs.
Viewers were asked to count the passes made by the team in white shirts.
Partway through, a person in a gorilla suit strolls into the middle of the game, thumps their chest and walks off.
It is on screen for several seconds.
Roughly half the viewers never saw it.
When told afterwards, many refused to believe it until they watched again, and some accused the researchers of swapping the tape.
The study has been repeated many times with similar results.
The lesson is unsettling: we do not see everything our eyes are pointed at.
Attention is a spotlight.
It feels as though we take in a whole scene in rich detail, like a camera.
We do not.
Your eyes send the brain more than it can process, so attention acts like a spotlight, picking out what seems relevant and leaving the rest dim.
Psychologists call failing to notice an unexpected object while focused on something else inattentional blindness, a term popularised by Arien Mack and Irvin Rock.
The missed object is in plain view.
What is missing is attention turning light into conscious experience.
A close cousin is change blindness.
In a 1998 study by Simons and Daniel Levin, pedestrians giving directions had the researcher swapped for a different person behind a passing door.
Around half did not notice.
Film continuity errors work the same way.
Even experts miss gorillas.
You might think trained professionals would be immune.
In a 2013 study, Trafton Drew, Melissa Vo and Jeremy Wolfe asked radiologists to search lung scans for small nodules that can signal cancer.
In the final case, the researchers had inserted a small image of a gorilla, many times larger than a typical nodule.
About four in five radiologists did not report it, even though eye tracking showed most had looked directly at the spot.
This does not mean radiologists are bad at their job.
They were brilliantly tuned to find nodules, and that is the point.
Expertise tells you where to look and what to look for, and anything outside that search template can slip by unseen.
Looked but failed to see.
Road safety researchers have a name for a common type of crash: 'looked but failed to see'.
A driver pulls out of a side street and hits a motorcyclist or cyclist, then insists they checked and the road was clear.
Often they are telling the truth as they experienced it.
Their attention was tuned to cars, so a smaller, less expected vehicle did not register.

Research by David Strayer and colleagues has found that phone conversations make this worse, and that hands-free calls are still distracting, because the problem is divided attention, not just your hands.
Australian road rules on phones vary by state, so check your state transport authority, but the psychology is the same everywhere.
Designing around blind spots.
Selective attention is what lets you function at all.
Imagine reading this sentence while consciously processing every sound, the feel of your clothes and every object in your peripheral vision.
Filtering lets you hold a conversation in a noisy cafe.
The cost is that it sometimes throws out something important.
People told about the gorilla in advance nearly always see it, but in a later Simons variation, those who knew the original gorilla were no better at spotting other unexpected changes.
So confidence is not evidence.
When driving, make a deliberate second look for bikes, motorbikes and pedestrians.
For important work, use checklists or a second pair of eyes.
Allow that two honest people can see different things.
The gorilla is always there somewhere; build systems that catch it.
The key idea: When we focus hard on one thing, we can miss something huge and obvious.
Quick recall. Answer out loud, or just in your head.
Question one. How does the brain handle memories?
Answer. It rebuilds them each time, so they can change.
Question two. Why do optical illusions work?
Answer. They exploit the brain's visual shortcuts.
Question three. What did the gorilla experiment show?
Answer. Focused attention can hide something large and obvious.
That's the end of this episode. The questions are waiting in your review, so you can lock in what you heard.
